utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. Have the witness brought in. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to apologise, the initial appearance took longer than had been expected. I'm very sorry. We are just chasing time, so that is yet one more reason to encourage you both, Prosecution and Defence, to try to move more quickly. All right, this is a public hearing, now, the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would, request, Mr. President, for the reasons stated yesterday, that the cross-examination proceed in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the reasons are for that, we are going to talk about Gomionica. I certainly don't want any harm to befall the witness, but I'm just telling you what we're going into at this particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well, do you have any specific reasons, Mr. Hayman? We seem to be constantly in closed session. Do you feel it's justified, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do, and I can go into greater detail, if you wish, in a closed session. But I think I stated the reasons earlier in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Hayman is relying on certain objections which he has already made or uncertain reasons which he has already advanced. Do you consider that those reasons pertain to the new field which you are now proposing to explore?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My answer to that, Judge Shahabuddeen, depends on a large part on the witness's answer. If the witness says he does know some things about what transpired, then I will explore what he knew, how he knew it, et cetera, you know, who told him, et cetera, some of the questions that I did before. But that, in large part, reflects my response to the witness's statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We don't have Judge Riad today who facilitates conversations on the bench. I'm unilingual, and Judge Jorda has made astonishing progress, as you have learned, in his command of the English language. Now, I am still dragging my feet in French, and that accounts for the peculiar disposition of the judges this morning, and the way we are sharing the microphone. What I wanted to ask you was this: The primary rule, is, of course, that proceedings in Court are in public. Very well, you made some objections yesterday, or you stated certain reasons yesterday in support of a motion for a closed hearing. The Prosecutor this morning says he proposes to explore a certain new area, and you have taken the position that reasons which you have given are equally applicable. May I suggest that the way ahead is this: That we allow the Prosecutor to begin in open session in a normal way, and if he comes to a crunch, then you rise and you repeat or renew your request for a closed hearing. And at that point the matter should be a lot clearer than it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Shahabuddeen, for your translation. All right, now we can resume. Thank you very much, Judge Shahabuddeen. It is very pleasant to work under conditions with colleagues such as Judge Shahabuddeen and Judge Riad, but we can now continue on the basis of what we just said. Have the witness brought in. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we're going to work for about 30 minutes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we're going to shift gears. We're going to remain on the 18th. Yesterday, just to bring us a little up to date, we talked about what was happening on the 18th in the Vitez area and Donja Veceriska, and I would like to shift gears to some of your testimony about what transpired in the Kiseljak area on the late night of the 17th of April and on to the day of the 18th of April and thereafter. Now, as we begin, I would like to address your attention back to a Defence document, and if we can begin with Defence document 258. Now, Brigadier, you identified Defence document 258 during the course of your testimony, I believe, where you identified it as a request for transportation by the British Battalion. This particular request for transportation picks Colonel Blaskic up in Kiseljak and brings him to Busovaca on the 12th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The text is illegible. I can read that on the 12th of April, 1993, security for the delegation of the HVO; so this is a request to provide transportation for an HVO delegation and their escort. There's also the time of departure, and also a request until 1600 hours, and a telephone number. So, it is a request for providing transportation, and it went to the British Battalion. I'm not sure who signed it. It seems to me it was Pircic, but I'm not too sure. The seal is from the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the English translation, if I can help you along a little bit, Brigadier, this document reflects that Blaskic is to be picked up at 0900 hours at the Kiseljak barracks on the 12th of April, 1993, on a Monday. I think everybody will agree that certainly that's the translation as is reflected in the French and the English. Now, that was a Monday. Let me show you a document, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 526, 526A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, without reading this whole document, as you can see, this is a document that is signed by Colonel Blaskic; is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by Colonel Blaskic, and these are my initials here, Slavko Marin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this particular document Blaskic is asked to be picked up on Friday, on the 9th of April, 1993, taken to Kiseljak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I realise there is no French copy, Judge, but I'm trying to expedite the questioning through the document. If Your Honour wants I can read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. Generally I say both to the Prosecution and the Defence, you have to be sure that the day that you make your final arguments, before the deliberations of the Trial Chamber, on that day, all documents that have not been translated into French be so. Let me tell you that now so you make the proper arrangements, because you still have several weeks, and enough time for it to be done. Continue please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, that indicates that Blaskic was taken down to Kiseljak on the 9th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this other document, which was offered by the Prosecutor, 256, it is obvious what it exactly says. From this document one cannot tell that General Blaskic will be travelling. So they are requesting two armoured personnel carriers for the transportation of the HVO military delegation and their escort on Friday the 9th of April. I did write this document, but indeed, I don't know whether any one of us officers travelled, either I or General Blaskic, because you cannot see it from here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the Defence document, 258, you stated in your direct that Blaskic is down in Kiseljak and is to be picked up on Monday, the 12th. Isn't it true, Brigadier, from this document you can indicate he got a lift down there on Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, the document that was offered by the Defence, as far as I can see, it also doesn't say that Blaskic is being transported. Again, reference is made to the delegation; and we did not ascertain, or deny, for that matter, that it was Blaskic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe. Try to be as complete as you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was Blaskic taken down to Kiseljak on Friday afternoon, the 9th of April, 1993, and was he picked up at Kiseljak barracks on the 12th of April, 1993, Monday morning at 9.00? That's the question. Was he or wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot confirm that, whether General Blaskic was taken exactly on that date. But I can confirm the following: That one could not go to Kiseljak, even if one wanted to, I mean the HVO members, from the January conflict. That is to say, after the BH army put under its control Kacuni and, therefore, the road, too. That is to say, without UNPROFOR participation and documents, it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do recall telling us in direct examination that quite often Blaskic went down to visit his family in the Kiseljak area and was taken down there by the British Battalion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I said. I said the following: That General Blaskic, before the conflict, that is to say, while one could take this road, while it was still accessible, he often went to see his family in Kiseljak. After the conflict, it was possible to reach Kiseljak only in UNPROFOR organisation, that is to say in this way; you had to submit a request and give the date and time and number of people and submit this request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the record will speak for itself. We will move on to the other documents. Let's turn to Defence document 299 and 300, both Defence documents. Before we go to that, Brigadier, you were the drafter of these, certainly of the order on the 8th of April; do you recall who was in this HVO military delegation and their escorts that was taken from Busovaca down to Kiseljak on the 9th of April? Do you recall who was in that delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly cannot recall who was on the delegation. But I believe that there are archives in the command of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Make an effort, General, please. You are the one who wrote the order. It involved the delegation, you, yourself, said you were not sure. But it's a very clear question, apparently on the 12th of April, Monday, Blaskic was in Kiseljak to go back to Busovaca, and then you wrote an order for the transportation of nine people. So it is a very simple question, was the accused one of them, yes or no? You are the one who wrote the order, you are number 2, you are right next to General Blaskic, you should know. Please answer, and then the Judges will make their evaluation. Yes or no, was the accused in that convoy for which you, yourself, drafted the order? You just said you drafted the order. You have a very faithful memory for several days. After all, he is the number one, he was your direct superior, you should have known whether or not he was there. Was he there or was he not there? It's a simple question. Was he in the convoy or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really cannot claim that General Blaskic was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, then, let's not be surprised that this cross-examination is taking so long. This is going to be Defence time, this is going to be counted as Defence time. Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move ahead and turn to Exhibits 299 and 300. Now, we start with 299 first, that is an order of Blaskic on the 17th of April, 1993 at 9.10 in the morning. If I can direct your attention to point 2b, "The order is given to the Ban Jelacic Brigade to take control of Gomionica and Svinjarevo after a strong artillery support by VBR and MB." My first question for you is: What is VBR and what is MB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: VBR is a multiple rocket launcher, and MB is a mortar. It doesn't say whether it's 82 or 102 millimetres, but it is a mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit 300, which is the next exhibit, and we can clarify exactly what type of artillery we're talking about. Again, this is an order written by you on the evening of the 17th of April, 1993, at 2345 hours. On point 2.2 in this order for combat operations you are giving instructions, "using all available artillery, carry out fire preparations for the attack from the VU," the abbreviation is unknown, "capture Gomionica and Svinjarevo through systematic targeting, 60, 80 and 120 millimetre mortar launchers." Is that, that's the type of artillery that was being used at that juncture; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the type of artillery that was supposed to be used for carrying out the assigned task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we previously noted that the taking of positions of artillery takes a high degree of planning, and I think you noted, and I can read your testimony to you, Brigadier, that "In order to launch artillery attacks, either from mortars, I don't know if it was calibre 80, 82 or 120, or from a rocket launcher, or from any other artillery piece, you need preparations. These preparations take a certain amount of time because the coordinates need to be established. The hits which were made show clearly," and you're talking about the hits that were taking place in Vitez. By the way, this is on page 12.301 of the Brigadier's direct testimony. So, the artillery preparations take a significant amount of time in order to be accurate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is why this preparatory combat command was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Let's continue on with what the events of that day, and let's move to Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/46. You previously talked about, and we discussed before, Exhibit 456/46 is an order going to Stjepan Tuka at 1.40 in the morning written by you with his combat assignments listed in point 2. That is: "Regroup the forces of your battalion and carry out combat operations on the village of Dusina or a breakthrough in the direction of the Busovaca stables and link with the forces defending Sebesic." Now, this was a two-pronged attack to be launched on the morning of the 18th with the Ban Jelacic Brigade taking over the areas of Gomionica and Svinjarevo while the Fojnica Brigade moved either towards Dusina or moved towards Sebesic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Ban Jelacic Brigade had as its task to link up the forces, in preparation and in execution it had the task of mastering Svinjarevo which is where the BH army units were located. The Battalion Fojnica also had the task of executing all operations to link forces in the places as quoted here. The reason for this was that the war was being waged in Busovaca and in Vitez, and that the forces coming as reinforcements should be linked up in that area. That is logical and is the military principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn or attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 510, if you could. Now, Prosecutor's 510 is the order to burn, number 3, the order of 27 January, 1993, and the last line on paragraph 3, the Bukovici village must be taken by nightfall on the condition that we burn anything standing in the way. Now, this is an order that is given by Mijo Bozic, the Ban Jelacic commander, and the person that was in charge was Mato Lucic, the brigade commander. That's what the document reflects. Let us turn our attention to Exhibits 305 and 306, Defence Exhibits 305 and 306.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we keep 510 with the Brigadier? That is the 27th of January, 1993 order, and I would like to let the Brigadier to look at the 27 January 1993 order in conjunction with Defence Exhibit 305 and 306.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the individual who gives this order to burn everything that is standing in the way on the 27th of January is Mijo Bozic, and the person in charge is Mato Lucic; those are the same two officers who are conducting operations in Kiseljak on the 18th of April 1993, aren't they? And if you want to refresh your recollection before you answer, I ask you to take a look at Defence Exhibit 305 and 306.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this document, 306, it was signed, that is, the name of the commander, Mijo Bozic, is on the name of the document, the document reached the Operative Zone command by a link packet, and on document 305 we have the operative officer in charge, the officer on duty, Mato Lucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the answer to my question is yes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection, the question was who launched the operations, and he said Mato Lucic was on duty at the command, in this way he is being led to give a false answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, he is not being led anywhere, and I will start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade commander in January who gave this order to burn everything in his way was Mijo Bozic; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade was Mijo Bozic. And to burn everything in the way, we discussed this, I cannot say that he was the commander of the brigade who gave the order to burn, what it stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brigade commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, on the 18th of April, 1993, who was on the receiving end of your combat orders, was the same man, Mijo Bozic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, now, let's move to Mato Lucic. On this order, on the 27th of January, which includes that the village, that anything should be burned standing in the way, the person in charge was Mato Lucic; isn't that right? And that is in number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With coordinating this operation which was ordered in document 510, and it stands that it should have been Mato Lucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to Exhibit 305. The individual that is reporting back about the combat operations in the Gomionica, Gromljak area, is the same man, Mato Lucic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but Mato Lucic, it is written here, is in the role of the officer on duty. That means somebody who, on the 18th of April, was on duty in the brigade. I don't know whether that was Mato Lucic, but I see from the document that it is; which means that he sits in the centre for 24 hours, takes in reports and assignments from commanders, what should be done from that position where he is on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, fulfilling the orders, let's move to Defence Exhibit 305, the one that comes from Mato Lucic, the officer on duty. And let's move to point B, where it talks about the enemy and MOS, the Muslim armed forces. "Our forces, which are fulfilling their task in the village of Gomionica, are being attacked. They are mostly using sniper rifles. A great number of forces has left Gomionica and pulled out towards the village of Stojkovici. "2. Our forces. Tasks are being done by orders. We have reached Mlava. Heavy fighting is going on. We are using artillery and means of PZO for support. Jehovac, Gromljak to Mlava and Palez have been disarmed. We have wounded people, we are going on with fulfilling our task. We have received zip from Fojnica bojna. Everything is ready. They're asking for negotiations. At this moment UNPROFOR came to the commander." My question on this is: At this particular time, on the 18th of April, 1993, at 1000 hours, the village of Jehovac and Gromljak have been disarmed, according to this report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The report that you have read out, I have not had in my hands, I have not had before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Usher, does the witness have 305.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is focused on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm that what is written here was done; namely, that they reached Mlava, that there was strong fighting and that artillery was used, as well as PZO for support, and that Jehovac, Gromljak up to Mlava and Palez had been disarmed, the place of Palez. So, there are wounded people, they are carrying on with fulfilling their tasks, and we have received zip, I suppose this is an abbreviation for telegram, from the Fojnica battalion saying everything is ready, and they are asking for negotiations, and all this linked to UNPROFOR. So, what is written in the report I cannot deny. It is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to Exhibit 306, the report that comes from Mijo Bozic, the Ban Jelacic Brigade commander. Do you have that sir, the report of the 18th of April, 1993 at 1645, which reads: "The conflict has spread to the villages of Rotilj, Visnjica, Doci, Hercezi and Brestovsko. We have lost Zavrtaljka." Pardon my pronunciation. "We did not manage to handle Gomionica, but we did take one kilometre on both sides around Gomionica. Heavy fighting is in progress. We have three killed and four wounded. The number of missing is unknown." My question for you, sir, is: It's pretty clear from this document that by 1645 on the afternoon of the 18th of April, 1993, combat operations are still taking place in the Gomionica, Gromljak area just north of Kiseljak; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, combat operations continued; isn't that correct, sir, through the night? And let me show you the 19th of April, 1993, a report from Mato Lucic at 0200 hours, and that would be Defence Exhibit 323. Without reading the whole document, again, this is another document coming from Mato Lucic in the early morning hours of the 19th of April, 1993. And on number 2, it says: "Our forces continue with intense activities in the Gomionica village since the MOS attempted a counter attack." Now, my question for you is: Throughout that whole day was there fighting in the Gomionica, Gromljak area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm only that what is written in the report is exact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a question. Let me show you Exhibit 293, Prosecution's Exhibit 293.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did I say 193? I meant 293, excuse me, 293.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a cease-fire document, Brigadier, that also came in, in the examination by the Defence. I'm not positive what the Exhibit number is on the Defence. But you testified that this cease-fire order on the 18th of April, 1993, was also written in BCS. And my question for you, Brigadier, is: You were in the headquarters at the time; was this sent to the Ban Jelacic Brigade during the 18th? Or were they told to ignore it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, 293, was signed by General Blaskic, the stamp is the Croatian community, but I can't see whether in Vitez. Have you got a Croatian version for me to read, so I can understand what is actually mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought that we would answer that question quickly, but it might be better to take a break. The interpreters have been working since 9.30 this morning, we are not going to begin again before a quarter to 3.00. Therefore, if you agree, Mr. Prosecutor, I'm sorry that I have to interrupt you, but we're going to suspend the hearing and we will start again at 2.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m. 25 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now, have the accused brought in, please, then the witness. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, while we're waiting for the witness, could we have Prosecutor's Exhibit 328, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution, you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prosecution, yes, sir. Mr. Dubuisson, it should be a map that looks like this. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier, we're resuming now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier. Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, some of the -- if you could move that down a little bit, we want to focus around, yeah, if we could just -- that's good. Brigadier, the attack in Kiseljak, or in the Gromljak, Gomionica area that we've been talking about on the 18th focused on the villages that we have on the ELMO, Prosecutor's Exhibit 328. And Gromljak, which you said was disarmed, and they were still attempting some fighting in Gomionica. And I believe in Defence exhibit 306 the fighting spread to Rotilj, Visnjica, Doci, Hercezi and Brestovsko; and these are villages, basically Muslim villages, that are located just north of the town of Kiseljak, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the structure of the population of Gomionica and Hercezi, but I do know that in Gomionica, according to our information, there was a stronger concentration of the BH army units, and that on the days that we mentioned, the 17th and 18th, there was intensive fighting there, which can be seen from the report by the operative on duty of the Ban Jelacic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the reports that you got from the Ban Jelacic Brigade, this fighting was taking place throughout the day on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fighting on the 18th, towards the 19th, that is to say, on the 18th -- perhaps it would be best if I had the report in front of me, but I'll try and recall this. It was waged for the reason, because the BH army units launched a counter-attack on the HVO units which were located in the immediate vicinity of Gomionica and the villages that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the reports, 305 and 306, which take us up to 1645 hours on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the report of the 18th of April, in point 2, and the report was written by the officer on duty, Mato Lucic. It states that execution of the assignment is described and that they had reached Mlava but there was intensive fighting, and that the guns were being used and the PZO as reinforcements, and Jehovac, Gromljak was disarmed, up to the village of Palez. We have wounded, and we are continuing the execution of our duties. We have received a zip from Fojnica, a telegram, and everything is ready, and they are calling for negotiations. I can go on reading the report where we see that on the 18th a counter-attack was carried out, and it was the report by the same officer on duty, because we're talking about the entirety of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What report are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right now I'm talking about the reports published on the 18th, and those are reports 305 and 306. Those are reports that are, the 18th at 10.00 in the morning, that's 305; and 306 is at 1645 on the 18th, written by Mijo Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I have the report by Mato Lucic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 18th, 19th, there is another report that we had before the break for lunch, it was on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was Defence Exhibit 323 of the 19th by Mato Lucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is 323.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report I asked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that is a report of 323 from 2.00 in the morning on the 19th. What time was this counter-attack that is referred in number 2 on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact time of the counter-attack, I don't know. If the report was written at 0200 hours, it would be logical to conclude that the counter-attack was before the report had been written. And it states clearly the positions from which the counter-attack was launched on the MOS, attempted by MOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using your logic, Brigadier, on the Exhibit 306, it would also be logical that the counter-attack took place after Mijo Bozic's report on the 18th of April, 1993 at 1645; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sometime between 1645 on the 18th and 2.00 in the morning on the 19th there was a counter-attack by the BiH. I would like to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 293.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The counter-attack, that is, according to the reports we have, the counter-attack took place in that time, that is, from the last report at 1645 to the report written at 0200 hours. That is what we can see from these two reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Exhibit 293, which is only in English, although you testified that you saw one in BCS on the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 293. However the same exhibit came in as a Defence exhibit, as well, and I'm just not certain what the Defence number is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a cease-fire agreement going to all subordinate HVO units to stop immediate combat operations. What time of day did this go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact time I cannot remember, but I do know that the order came from the main staff and that it was on the basis of the agreement reached by President Boban and President Izetbegovic, and that a cease-fire was ordered, and that on the basis of that order we wrote this order, number 293, that that order had gone, had been dispatched to the HVO units and also to the monitoring mission. This report by Mato Lucic on the 19th of April at 200 hours, he is informing the commander why, in addition to this report, fighting was still carried on, because the MOS forces had launched a counter-attack. And so, the cease-fire was not abided by. And I should like to remind you, Mr. President, that when I spoke about the 19th, I remember very well, and I have facts here before me, that on the 19th, that is to say, in spite of the cease-fire order which was issued, that on the 19th the most intensive attacks took place in the Busovaca municipality. The events that followed, that is to say, when these orders on a cease-fire were not recognised by the army in the Kiseljak area, because it felt itself to be strong and wanted to achieve its goals, on the 20th, General Petkovic came and General Halilovic and the meeting Zenica was held as to establish that cease-fire. But on that, neither on that day, the 20th, was this recognised, because I remember the event when General Blaskic went to Zenica and when the BH units in the Vitez area launched an attack on the line. And so, all this, these documents can be understood within the framework of the overall activities that took place at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this order sent to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, the cease-fire order? The Prosecutor's Exhibit 293, which for the record, Mr. President, is Defence Exhibit 318, it's the same document. Was the Ban Jelacic Brigade told on the 18th that a cease-fire order had been signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what General Blaskic did, orders of this kind, which came from subordinates, would be sent out to all the commands and that would include the Ban Jelacic Brigade and that is why in point 2 in the report, which was written at 2.00 a.m., the officer on duty states that an attempt was made at a counter-attack. A counter-attack was attempted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There has been a mistranslation. It says that reports that were received from subordinates were sent by Blaskic to subordinate units, so this is a mistranslation. The witness said the orders they received from superiors he always sent to subordinates, so would you please correct this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No problem. Registrar, did you take note of that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the fact that Mr. Nobilo has indicated the error means that it would automatically be corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were orders given by Blaskic for the Ban Jelacic Brigade to cease operations upon receipt of Exhibit 293, which is Defence Exhibit 318, and to cancel the previous outstanding combat orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in addition to this cease-fire order, there were additional orders written by Blaskic telling the Ban Jelacic Brigade to cease all offensive activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This order that went to the European Monitoring Mission and to the 3rd Corps of the BH army went to our units, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, based on this order, did the Ban Jelacic Brigade cease combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this report and upon receiving this order, one can see exactly what the Ban Jelacic Brigade is doing. So, in point one it says that the Chetniks were not in operations, that Muslim forces were continuing to engage targets from the region of Gomionica to the best of our knowledge and they attempted attacks which they repelled, so the obviously the counter-attack would not have been repelled if there had not been fire. INTERPRETER: The witness is reading too fast for the interpreters, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier, you have to slow down a bit so the interpreters can keep up with you. I didn't mean to interrupt you, just slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the 18th, 1993, 18th of April 1993, the activities of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, according to this report, were as follows: They report to us that the Chetniks, that is to say, the army of Republika Srpska was not operating because the Ban Jelacic Brigade, at that time, had that front-line, too, that the Muslim forces continue to operate from small arms from the region of Gomionica on the positions of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, against. Now, further on, they tried to launch a counter-attack from the village of Gomionica, and it was repelled. Further on, in the region of Pobrdje, the Muslim forces, that is to say, the BH army, engaged targets among our forces, and further on it says that our units, that is to say, the units of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, continue their operations against Gomionica intensely, why? Because the units of the BH army tried to launch a counter-attack. So, he is informing the commander that he is involved in war operations. He is waging war for such and such reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of questions about what you just said. And you noted at the outset that against the Serbs there was no combat activities in the brigade zone. My question for you is, was the HVO at Kiseljak cooperating with the Bosnian Serb army at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I'm not aware of whether the HVO co-operated with the units of the army of Republika Srpska, but during 1993, when Kiseljak and the area around Kiseljak were fully surrounded, according to the information that I had at that time, that is to say, for purposes of logistics and supplies, the HVO did cooperate with the army of Republika Srpska, with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in a bit, sir, but staying with Exhibit 323, the 19 April 1993 report of Mato Lucic at 3.00 in the morning, it does note at point 2, "our forces continue with intense activities in the village of Gomionica since MOS Muslim armed forces, attempted a counter-attack." Now, at the same time on the 19th, you are still expecting the offensive to be taking place by the Fojnica Brigade against either Dusina or against Sebesic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If possible, could I get the orders that Fojnica Brigade got so that I know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir, 456/48. And while we're there, this is Prosecution Exhibit 456/48, 456/49 and 456/50, and we can move through these quickly. Looking at 456/48, which is the order that you wrote to the commander of the Fojnica battalion, Stjepan Tuka, on the 19th of April 1993 at 1800 hours, you are telling him to comply with the orders issued by Mijo Bozic, commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says here that will be issued. That is something that is supposed to happen. In the Croatian language it says that will be issued, rather, not that was issued by the Ban Jelacic Brigade, commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Brigadier, I have a different translation, and maybe it's a interpretation problem, but my translation says, "Owing to the difficult situation and the open aggression of the Muslim forces, I call to your attention your duty to execute and comply with the orders issued by the commander of the Ban Jelacic, Kiseljak Ban Jelacic Brigade." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's a mistranslation. The right way to put it is "with the orders to be issued by the commander of the Kiseljak Ban Jelacic Brigade," that is to say, that will be issued by the commander, not those that were already issued. And it is only logical, because until then Ban Jelacic Brigade, did not command this battalion. Until then this battalion was under the command of Nikola Subic-Zrinski, so Ban Jelacic was not in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, orders were given to the Fojnica Brigade on 1.40 on the 18th of April 1993, and was given a specific assignment, and I'm looking at Exhibit 456/46, telling the Fojnica Brigade what to do. If there is a mistranslation, there is a mistranslation. I can tell the Court, I think, that I'm faithfully reading what has been translated. Nevertheless, the Fojnica Brigade was giving orders at 1.40 in the morning on the 18th. And, at this point, on the 19th of April 1993, did you have information that Stjepan Tuka had refused to comply with your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 19th, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From document 458/48, which I wrote, it is obvious that the commander is warning commander Tuka, the commander of the Fojnica unit, that he is duty-bound to carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it's logical, is it not, Brigadier, that the commander and you had information that Tuka was not complying with what Colonel Blaskic wanted him to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he refused to carry out orders that were given to him. And I think that the Prosecutor offered this into evidence and we can see exactly what was ordered and what he refused to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did you get that information from the Ban Jelacic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that this order was not carried out, I can't remember who we received it from, but I know that it was not carried out. I think that in the Prosecutor's documents it was also offered that, you know, this could not be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you, Brigadier, is: Were you getting other information from the Ban Jelacic Brigade, other than the three reports that we have introduced into evidence, and the Defence exhibits that have been introduced into evidence, and we can clarify that, it is Exhibit 305, 306 and 323?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether we got other reports, but the contents of these reports show, evidently, that they show the most important events taking place at the time of these operations of the Ban Jelacic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's be very specific about this. You are now the deputy commander, because commander Nakic is not there, and you're also the Chief of Staff. Is it your testimony that you do not recall any other information coming from the Ban Jelacic Brigade other than these three reports that we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly cannot recall the document as such, but if I were to see this document, to see its contents, I would know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you one, and this is only one, and I ask to you take a look at 456/49, and this is an order of Colonel Blaskic of 19 April 1993 at 1845.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, excuse me, Prosecution Exhibit 456/49, I think he has that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, but it's not in its Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if we can, I think there should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we have it translated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It has been translated in French and English, the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But all the 456 documents, I don't have all of them with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 456 should be an order of Blaskic, 19 April 1993 at 1845. That's it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the document that was issued at 1845 is called 458, the one I have here. Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you check that, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it's 456.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine says 458, the 19th of April 1993 at 1845.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I trust we have clarified any confusion on 456 or 458, the document, trust me, it's 456.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now it says 456.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're all singing off the same sheet of music, so to speak. Now, the beginning of that letter says -- this is something going to, an order going to the Ban Jelacic Brigade and it says, "reference your letter 22-04-93". So, this order is in response to a communication that comes from the Ban Jelacic Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If we want to speed things up, if it's clear, there's no point to say it, you can say, it simply says your letter number, such and such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm saying to you is, during this fighting, in the Gomionica and in the Gromljak area, this order of Colonel Blaskic verifies that you were getting additional information from the Ban Jelacic Brigade; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, from this document it is obvious that another letter had arrived, 22/04/93, if I were to see that, I would remember. But, from this text, which is a reply to that letter, one may assume what the original letter had said, especially if we bear in mind the date, April 19, 1993, when there is heavy fighting around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this particular document in number 1 says, and we won't read the whole matter, says "you must go on because the Croatian people has no other choice," grammatically that's incorrect, "the Croatian people have no other choice for the time being," and on five it says, "the future of all Croats of Busovaca, Travnik, Vitez and Novi Travnik depend on your success. Whereas in Zenica and any concentration camp, particularly Gornji Zenica, where our people who have fled from the centre at Zenica are being slaughtered. Every day, there is a massacre." Now, let me refer you to the next exhibit that has been given to you, which is 456/50, and that is an order of Blaskic on the 19th of April 1993 at 2140 hours, several hours after the previous exhibit. Do you see that, Brigadier? Now, it would appear from that there has been yet another communication coming from the Ban Jelacic Brigade, because this order references a report coming from the Ban Jelacic Brigade and Blaskic's response is, "You must take Gomionica tonight or in the early morning, because the main forces of the Muslim armed forces are at Busovaca, which is being attacked today by the main forces of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although certainly unsuccessful. They are also attacking Vitez and destroying it by all means." So, the order specifically is to take Gomionica by the early morning, and this is in reply to a report that was received by the headquarters as to what was going on; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reply is given on the basis of the document that had arrived from the Ban Jelacic Brigade. The objective is to engage forces, to engage forces. Because under point 1 it says, "You must take Gomionica tonight or in the early morning because the main forces of the MOS are at Busovaca," and I already mentioned that, "which is being attacked today by the main forces of the 3rd Corps," that is to say after the order issued by Petkovic and Halilovic on the 19th, attacks are being launched against Busovaca. But it is certain that it is unsuccessful, that is to say, that the General is encouraging his men. Of course, he is not going to tell his men, "You are going to fall, we are going to fall." Of course, he wants to encourage them. However, they are also attacking Vitez and destroying it by using all means. If you halt the attack, we will be subjected to strong assaults and will be destroyed, bit by bit. Now, what does this say? "If in Kiseljak and in Fojnica the units of the HVO do not engage, do not go into combat with army units." We have to understand that this is a distance of five or ten kilometres, all these forces will be aimed against Busovaca, Busovaca will fall and after the fall of Busovaca Kiseljak would fall, too, and then Vitez would fall, and so on and so forth. That is the essence of this order, this is the core of the matter and that is what the order of the commander of the brigade of Ban Jelacic was aiming at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the bottom line is that the headquarters in Vitez was getting additional information from the Ban Jelacic Brigade that was happening and what was going on in the Gomionica area, other than the reports that we have seen in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that two letters have arrived and they state what is happening and how it is happening and it is quite logical that these two documents were sent, because the cease-fire order was given by the commander. However, the results were as they -- as we know they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I highlight this because during your direct testimony you said these three reports were the only three reports you got from the Ban Jelacic Brigade discussing the conflict. And we have at least two other references to information where Blaskic received additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like to ask that if something is shown to the witness and that that has been stated, that it be quoted, because as far as I remember, the witness said that in the contents, the information that was received, he did not say that he received only three papers. So, would you read what he actually said and quote him, if you are quoting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the break I will go get the transcript about what was actually said about these transcripts. At this point I will move on about what this witness said about the information. Suffice it to say, I think you would agree with me, Brigadier, that the headquarters was receiving more information than the three reports that were submitted during the testimony in Defence. Now, let's look back at this particular map, which is Prosecution Exhibit 328.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, these orders back and forth to go on and take Gomionica by the morning time, they were sent to the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, Mijo Bozic, who had discussed that, we discussed previously in Exhibit 510, as giving that order to burn everything in his path as they took Bukovci. But look at Prosecution Exhibit 95. But before we do that, do you know exactly what happened during these attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. President, the order mentioning the burning was an order dating back to January and we're now speaking about April. And in order for me to answer your questions precisely, I would like to know the exact time and the month we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think the witness is right, this has to be properly identified, otherwise there is going to be confusion. The order that you're alluding to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mijo Bozic wrote that order in January saying, "that in taking Bukovci, Bukovci must be taken by night fall on the condition that we burn everything our path." We have established that according to your testimony, Brigadier. And the same commander was the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade when the attack ensued on April the 18th of 1993. I think we have concluded that, as well, Brigadier. My question to you is: What happened to those villages as a result of that attack that took place on the 18th and 19th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Gomionica was not -- that is to say, Gomionica was not placed under the HVO control, and that the Gomionica area and Svinjarevo lines were established, which short deviations were there until the Washington Accords. Mr. President, I cannot agree with the observation of the Prosecutor when talking about the January order. In fact, I said what I know, and I said that those villages were not taken, and that what was written by Mijo Bozic had not, in fact, been executed. I can just add that the kind of language used was not the kind of language usually used, and I know General Blaskic well enough to know his style of writing, and I know he would never sign to any, an order written by any of us written in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You made the clarification you wanted to. The document can be interpreted in several ways. All right, what you said will be taken into account. Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let us look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 95 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we still on the same subject, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us read Prosecutor's Exhibit 95, this is a daily report that came from the European Commission Monitoring Mission signed by Alan Lawstone and Lars Driversen to RC Zenica, Team Z1, "daily report, 29 April 1993, together with an armed escort from CANBAT, Canadian battalion, the team visited Polje Visnjica, Vecesi (phoen), Doci, Visnjica and Gomionica. Findings: Polje Visnjica, the team was stopped at the HVO checkpoint, mines were pulled out in front of the team and the checkpoint behaved threateningly with RPG 7 in firing position. Checkpoint demand to see ID, and search the APCs before we were allowed to pass."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If it's for me, thank you, but the registrar lent me his copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I just go down to the individual conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Most of the Muslim houses have been burned and all the Muslims have left the village. There are still Croat families in the village. Hercezi, a few Muslim families had returned after the fighting had ended. There are good relations to the Croat neighbourhood, no burned houses, 14 killed in Hercezi, Polje Visnjica area. Doci, village was left -- village were left, only a few burned houses. Visnjica, 40 out of 150 Muslim houses were burned, five men were killed at the field, approximately 20 Muslim families have turned to the village. There are still Croat families in the village. The Muslims are not confident with the neighbours. Note, none of the Muslims in the above-mentioned villages are allowed to pass through the checkpoint at Polje Visnjica. Gomionica, today the team could visit the village without any problems. The village are left and totally destroyed. HVO soldiers with RPGs and a few snipers were observed pursuing the team. Protest, the team want to protest because of the behaviour at the HVO checkpoint where our interpreter was threatened, as well as the search for the APCs, of the APC. Team conclusion, it is obvious that an ethnic cleansing had taken place." So at least in the village of Gomionica and in addition to these other villages, at least in the village of Gomionica, the village was totally destroyed, and this was at the hands of the Ban Jelacic Brigade. Was that information conveyed to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This report, that is to say its contents, are not known to me. The village of Gomionica we saw from reports hitherto that there was very intensive fighting there and the consequences of that fighting in these villages I have not had information about. I did not have information about how many houses were burned of both sides, how many people remained, where those people are now, the people who had left, and the military information, and for me as an operations man, it was important for me to know where the positions were, when the fighting was taking place, what the HVO units were controlling, what the BH army units were controlling, and what we could expect in the time to come. I do not deny all these facts that have been enumerated here because I truly do not know the consequences and the results that ensued after the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a photograph that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 391, and it is a fold-out photograph of the remnants of the village of Gomionica that looks like this. And as the witness is looking at it, Mr. President, I will gladly hand my copy up to Your Honours. Mr. Usher, if we could give this to the Judges, and the other exhibit goes to --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is in the vault at the moment. Can we take a few moments to go get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think after the Judges get through, or the witness can use the Defence copy, thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that is a photograph that has been identified as the village of Gomionica, these photographs are taken in approximately May of 1996. Are you familiar with this village, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the village of Gomionica, because it is a village in the Kiseljak municipality and I cannot, on the basis of this photograph, state whether it is the village of Gomionica or some other village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you said that, with regard to the report that we had, concerning what happened in Gomionica in April of 1993, that you have no reason to doubt the reports of the European Commission Monitoring Mission. My question for you is: Do you know anybody, any member of the HVO that was ever punished or disciplined for what happened in the ethnic cleansing that took place in this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, once again an erroneous interpretation. The witness said that he does not doubt now as to the report of the European Monitors, and he saw the report for the first time now, ten minutes ago. He did not get the report in 1993. The Prosecutor seems to say that he received the report earlier on and wants to know what Blaskic did in the way of disciplinary action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe. I think that the difficulty that we are running into and have been ever since the beginning, I've said it several times, is that the witness has memory problems, and we have seen that, which is -- and that makes the cross-examination more difficult. Your task was easier because the witness was prepared within the context of your own intentions and objectives, but now it's more complicated. The difficulty of the cross-examinations have to be found right at that point. It's true, but I cannot say that the Prosecutor's comments are not legitimate. I've often said this witness is in the number 2 position in charge of operations and we're talking about operations. Once again, he cannot both remember everything when he was testifying for you and then not remember anything when he was testifying for the Prosecutor. He was the number 2 operational person. You're the one who called him in. He didn't see the report, but there was an ECMM report. Perhaps he didn't see the report, but he cannot contest the contents; therefore, once he doesn't contest it, it is not illegitimate to ask whether there were or were not sanctions. I'm sorry for interrupting, but I've said it several times, this is the difficulty we that we're finding in this testimony. We have to be patient. What else can we do? Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe, it's legitimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, based on the ethnic cleansing in the Gromljak and Gomionica area in April of 1993, was any HVO soldier, either prosecuted in the military courts or disciplined in the discipline courts as a result of his actions in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot agree with the observation of ethnic cleansing. We have seen up to now that wherever there was fighting, with all the consequences, the burning of houses, a large number of dead, that if the place was taken control of by the HVO units, that from that place, locality, with the BH units, the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina left, and if the settlement was taken over by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army units, the Croatian population would withdraw from those areas and would follow the HVO. Why? Because they felt themselves to be insecure, and we saw the amount of problems that existed and what the people had to live through if they stayed on in the settlements where their army was not in control. For that reason, I cannot, within this context, give an answer and say "yes", or "no", in the context of observing that ethnic cleansing had been conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your question again, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you know of any HVO soldier that was prosecuted, either in the disciplinary courts or in the military courts of justice as a result of his actions in the Gromljak and the Gomionica area in April of 1993? Do you know of anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not know, but I would like to take advantage of this question to tell the Judges, as far as I'm able, of the situation and circumstances in which these terrible actions took place, which I denounce, absolutely. Mr. President, in Bosnia, where the war was being waged, everything that was committed, that -- everything that was committed in the sense of house burning, or some other inhumane acts was -- it was very difficult to arrive at a name, and we have not arrived at a name to this day. Now, why is that so? I'm telling you my opinions and my vision of the situation, because I was there, I spent some time there, and I would like to explain why that is so. We said how the units were set up, what the family relationships were, the neighbourly relations were. Nobody wanted to disclose any names. I am now asking myself the question, what would I have done had I been commander of the Operative Zone in a situation of this kind when you cannot get any name or surname of any individual committing acts of this kind? I remember one particular example, and that is that on one occasion a judge, whether it was the judge of a military court or not, but somebody in the Lasva River Valley, that he was shot at in the legs. They shot at his legs. And after an incident and a row that had broken out in the settling of accounts between individuals. That is to say, after weapons had been used. And when one of these was wounded, and ten days later that individual who had wounded that particular man was himself killed. Mr. President, it is because of the gravity of the war in Central Bosnia, in the war between the BH army units and the HVO that it is very difficult to arrive at any names, and we have not been able to come by the names today. Nobody wants to state those names. As far as the burning of houses is concerned and all other acts, they did not -- were not done following orders. These were not acts that were done in an organised fashion, but they were done so that there was no information and no knowledge of the acts committed and of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, based on what you just said, did General Blaskic and the others in the headquarters know that this type of burning of civilian houses was taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did General Blaskic know that on the day when it happened, that I do not know. But I believe that as time went by he, afterwards, did receive information on what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when he received that information, did you see any orders that Blaskic gave to investigate what happened in those villages in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my answer has been understood wrongly. It's not that I said that we received written information, I simply believed that after sometime, after a day, two days, three days, five days, 20 days, and I believe this was also mentioned during the peace talks, I imagine that when the consequences of this war were mentioned and when the senselessness of this war was expounded on, that this was mentioned, too. I did not receive any written information from the Ban Jelacic Brigade on the consequences of this war or rather the consequences of these combat operations on the territory of Gomionica and that is why I'm saying that this is the first time, at this point in time, when I read this report of international organisations that I come across this information for the very first time. And that is equally true for all places where there was combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier, I think that everything you have said has been noted down. The Tribunal will note with interest what you said. As regards your conception of ethnic cleansing, the judges will make their evaluation when it comes to knowing exactly what ethnic cleansing is. As for the rest, one can say that for your morning briefings you did not speak about the most recent developments, what was happening on the ground in that period when there was a briefing in the morning. I suppose there must have been -- did what was happening a few kilometres from there, was it spoken about? Was there nobody who said they were burning houses? I'm not asking whether it was Croatian or Muslim, nobody said they were burning houses? You are the number 2 operative person, but nobody said, "Well, you know, Colonel, in Gomionica there were houses that were burned?" I'm not setting a trap for you. You just said there was no conferences, no meetings in the headquarters in this time of war saying that in Gomionica there were houses that were burning, but we had to wait for several years until that information was given. We will note what you said and we will ask Mr. Kehoe to continue. We can't do anything more than note what you yourself have said. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a few more sentences about this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that after a few years, General Blaskic found out about this. I did not say that he found out after five days. The consequences of the war in many localities were such or similar. Perhaps in Gomionica things were a bit harsher, but in many villages it was similar to this, or like this, wherever there was fighting between the HVO and the army. Truth to tell, during the fighting, if a village was burned down, and if there were 50 houses, perhaps ten houses might have been burned during the fighting, however, during 1993, that is to say, all the events that took place, all the battles that took place, all the consequences of these battles, led to the fact that five or ten houses would be burned down during the night. How would this happen? I shall give you an example of something I saw with my very own eyes. For example, Bucegori (phoen), that is village where Croats lived and it is a village on top of a hill, and you can -- it's Bosniaks who live there and then there is no fighting, but they torch one Croat house. Then somebody sees this, and somebody else who assumes whose house this is, perhaps torches five other Muslim houses. Or, for example, a man gets killed, for example, my brother gets killed or one of your nearest and dearest, and since you're so nervous and everything, this happens again. Everything that we see in this picture today, Mr. President, does not have to be a fact, although I'm not saying that it is not a fact. It does not have to be due to a conflict itself. Torching houses is a problem that we used to encounter and that we could not overcome throughout 1993, even though settlements that remained under HVO control. But it was likewise in those places that were under the control of the units of the BH army. And when you put all these figures together about the total number of houses burned down, which is the greatest tragedy and the greatest harm of all, all of this speaks of the fact that what I'm saying is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. The clarification has been taken into account and the Judges will evaluate them at proper time. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, Mijo Bozic was the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade during this time, and during this same time, or maybe in early May, did information come to the Hotel Vitez that Mijo Bozic was signing eviction notices that were given to Bosnian Muslims for them to be evicted from their premises in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have such information. But, Mr. President, we often mention Mijo Bozic here. Mr. President, the name of Mijo Bozic we often mention here, and I want to tell you more about the person whom I know. That is a man who certain disobedient people kicked out of the brigade in May, and after that, another person came to lead the brigade, and what am I trying to say? That man did not have the kind of authority that the commander of a brigade was supposed to have. It's not for want of expertise, but simply that was the situation at that time. I would have been the happiest of all if this were not the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to add a footnote, Mr. President. We heard the testimony about these supposed notices many months ago and they pertained to state-owned apartments, that was omitted from Mr. Kehoe's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can check the record. There is a document under seal if counsel wants to check it right now. It's Exhibit 461 and the page is 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I remember the testimony, Mr. President, from the witness, in the transcript, state-owned apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would invite the Court to look at the transcript and I invite the Court to look at the exhibit and I cite the place in the exhibit, again. It's document under seal Exhibit 461, page 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, Mijo Bozic, the man you just talked about, was the man you talked at the outset of your testimony as one of the three individuals with military training as a graduate of the Military Academy, as was the defendant, Blaskic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't deny it, but I just wanted to say what his true authority was, and how much he could actually give orders. They kicked him out of the command, literally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the man that was given the command in the Ban Jelacic Brigade, and who also was the Chief of Operations before you were the Chief of Operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of that is correct. No one contested Bozic's expertise and I never said it. But being Mijo Bozic with an academy degree is one thing, that is to say with formal training and a formal post and position, that is one thing, but another thing is to rule in a situation as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when was Mijo Bozic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's go on. We're getting lost here. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Mijo Bozic replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mijo Bozic was expelled on the 10th of May 1993 from the command, literally. And that is what I found out after the war, and people made fun of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was replaced by Ivica Rajic, again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic came to replace Mijo Bozic, that is to say that Mijo Bozic was replaced without anyone having asked General Blaskic whether Mijo Bozic could be replaced or not. And nobody even asked him, so General Blaskic could only nod his head at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's talk about the 19th and we can move ahead to another subject, Mr. President. We will go from the 19th and move into the Vitez area, and during the course of the 19th, you didn't discuss in your direct testimony the fact that the town of Zenica was shelled on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, just a moment, we have been here since a quarter to three, since we're moving from the 18th of April, I suggest that we take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, as I noted before the break, we are going to move back to the Vitez, Zenica area for the 19th of April, 1993. The first question --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you excuse me for a moment, I don't see anything on the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to suspend the hearing for a few moments. (Technical interruption)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we're going back, as I said, we are going back to the Vitez, Zenica area for the 19th of April, 1993, and that was the day that Zenica was shelled at approximately noontime; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I heard Zenica was shelled, I don't know whether on the 19th or the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of artillery pieces did the Central Bosnian Operative Zone have on the 19th, what calibre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we had a Howitzer 122 millimetres and a Howitzer 152 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these two Howitzers positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were positioned in the area of the village of Puticevo and in the area of the Mali Mosulj village, or more exactly, the facility, the coming along facility. And the local population called this the Pleseba (Phoen), the stone quarry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they mobile? In other words, did they have wheels on them that could be carried around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That possibility did exist, but they were more massive artillery pieces, and for that kind of activity, a certain amount of time would be needed. I can't tell you how much time, because I'm not an expert gunner, but it is massive artillery, and massive weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Puticevo; are you talking about Novi Travnik, in the Novi Travnik area, where one of those weapons was positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the area of Puticevo, this is an area along the road towards Travnik. The closest bigger place is Dolac, the closest towards Travnik, and the other neighbouring place is, and the ratio is 1 to 50.000, on the map is upper and lower Puticevo. I can show you on the map, if you have a map available. I'm quite ready to point out the position of Puticevo. But the exact position, give or take 50 metres or so, and the artillery pieces, I could not tell you that exactly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These artillery pieces were under the direct command of Colonel Blaskic; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that they were not under his command, these artillery pieces. They were under the artillery division, and that division had a commander, and the commander was directly under the command of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, which piece that you were talking about, either the 122, and I think you said it was a 155 or a 152, which piece was at Puticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, at Puticevo it was the 122 piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you recall that day that the actual shelling of Zenica took place, where civilians were killed in Zenica, and you recall that the Central Bosnian Operative Zone and the HVO were blamed for that shelling; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that I have about that, and as far as I know, and as far as I knew in those days, I don't know the exact day. That is what I know today. I heard this via the Bosnian radio station, that Zenica was shelled. And that shelling was explained in such a way, that is to say, information and propaganda wise, and in the announcement that I heard over Zenica radio, the speaker making the announcement maintained, and let me try and remember the term he used, that the Ustashe had shelled Zenica. That is what he said, more or less, to that effect.
