Because in the war that we had with the BH army, that is to say, in communications, and certain information services of the BH called the HVO the Ustashe. And this term was used in the radio announcement over radio Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this issue discussed in the morning meetings with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, after the information via the public media which I had, I don't know exactly how General Blaskic came by this information that we were being blamed for something of that kind, that he contacted the commander of the division and asked him whether he had done this on his own, independently, because he could not have done so without orders from the commander. My information is that the commander of the division said that he had not done this, and as far as I know, we from the command of the Operative Zone never issued an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did Blaskic take his commander's word for it, or did he do any type of investigation to determine whether or not the, either the 122 or the 155 had fired onto Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An investigation in that case, when you are not, when you cannot be on the spot to perform a ballistic expertise to see what direction, what calibre was used, and so on; in the sense that you ask, it was not possible to undertake an investigation of that kind. And in conditions of that kind, if the commander asks his subordinate whether he did that or not, the commander must believe his subordinate if he tells him he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To add a few words. In addition to this, did General Blaskic go into further contact with the commander? I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of further such activity. Because I said how and in which way I received certain pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did Blaskic contact the 3rd Corps and request to do a joint investigation with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to determine who fired these shells into Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Blaskic had some contacts with the representatives of UNPROFOR, whether with Mr. Stewart or one of his associates linked to the implementation of that activity. What Stewart or some of his associates told him with regard to that issue, I do not know. I know that General Blaskic, as far as I recall, went to a meeting in Zenica on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is, did he contact, to your knowledge, as chief of operations, and during this time as the deputy Chief of Staff, did Blaskic contact 3rd Corps, or anyone in 3rd Corps to attempt to do a joint investigation to determine if this had been fired by an HVO artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that, and I cannot either confirm or say no to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at this time there were joint investigations going on between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct? And I refer you to Defence Exhibit 303, if I may show that to the witness. This is a document that you discussed during your direct examination from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik that takes place on the 18th of April, 1993. It's a report from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade to the headquarters, and it talks in the opening paragraph about a joint investigation on the kidnapping of the officers from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. So, during this period of time, joint investigations between the HVO and the ABiH were taking place. The opening line says "Further to the work of the HVO and the Bosnia-Herzegovina army joint commission on investigating the kidnapping of officers from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade on 13 April, 1993." And then it discusses how the two entities are working together to attempt to solve this, and travelling to places to attempt to solve it. And my question for you, Brigadier, was: You, as the Chief of Staff, the deputy Chief of Staff at time, and the chief of operations; do you know of any requests that went from the headquarters to 3rd Corps to attempt to do a joint investigation like was taking place in Novi Travnik with the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The activities with regard to investigation and joint investigation of the shelling in Zenica at this time and on this date, I do not know about. But the document that you have proffered as an explanation testifies to an act and a commission which was set up to deal with that particular case, and that is what is written in the preamble. And it says, with regard to the joint work of the joint commission of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to throw more light on the case of the kidnapping of the officers. So, this commission dealt with that particular case and those problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, Brigadier, is: Was there any attempt by Blaskic, during this time frame, when he attempted to do a joint investigation with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to discover who shelled Zenica? And my reference point for you is this particular document where we have established that joint investigations were taking place. I'm just asking you, did that request take place by Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has already answered. The Prosecutor asked him earlier on whether he knows that Blaskic moved any form of investigation with the 3rd Corps and the witness said he did not know, he cannot either confirm or deny it, so this is just a repetition of the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Nobilo is right, the question was answered, was asked, you got your answer, apparently he does not know very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of time, Brigadier, the HVO had the capability, through electronic surveillance data, to determine where a particular weapon was fired from and who fired on an area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly do not know of this, but I'm trying to think as a commander would think about this case in its entirety. And if you know that General Blaskic knew that this was shelling, and then there is no need to make any great initiative for this to be confirmed. I'm thinking about what I would have done had I been the commander. If I knew that I did not do something, and the International Community and through its mediation or the representative of the 3rd Corps are not offering an initiative along those lines in that direction, I don't know why, then, I, myself, alone should confirm this. This is what I'm saying on my own personal thoughts in the matter, had I been commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the HVO, or do you not know whether or not they had the capability through electronic surveillance to determine the place where shells had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that we had this kind of technical possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you were aware of the technical capability of the HVO. I'm getting concerned. You say you didn't know anything about, occasionally you said you didn't know anything about the technical capabilities, several times you said you're not aware of this or that capability; but you did have a role which would seem to indicate that you were aware of certain technical capabilities. Isn't that right? Really, you're beginning to worry me. You were never in the right briefing, you don't know if there were briefings or if there was strategic material. The question was very specific. Were you aware of the technical material? Was there any or was there not any? So, you continue to say that you were not aware? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really don't know of that kind of equipment, because in the affairs we had, we had a commander for the gunnery section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm noting that, but with a great deal of interest. Very frequently you are not aware of anything. It's been noted down. You really have got blanks in your memory, but not -- it's somewhat worrisome, that is what I wanted to say to you. It's my right as a Judge to be able to say this All right, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if there is a linguistic issue here. I think the witness, to a number of questions, is saying "not that I know of," which is different from "I don't know". But when the witness says "not that I'm aware of," that doesn't mean he is having a lapse of memory, unless the question, the fact being asserted in the question is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, he says he is not aware. My comment was that I was surprised that the number two to chief of operations is not aware of the technical capabilities of the military equipment. It was surprise that I was expressing, and I was saying I had the right to be surprised, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, there are two different possible answers. "I don't know" or "not that I'm aware of." The witness could also say "no." Those are three different answers, but "not that I'm aware of" is different than "I don't know," and let's look at -- I would propose, let's look at the document. We don't know, I don't know if the HVO had this capability. I think the witness is saying, "if we did, I wasn't aware of it." That may be shocking, but it's only shocking if in fact they had this capability, whatever it is, that is being loosely referred to as electronic surveillance. That was my comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for your comment. Perhaps we will allow the Brigadier, who is your witness, to make even a greater effort to jog his memory about the technical capabilities of the operational units of which he was the number two in the accused's staff. Continue, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could show this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I? It was interpreted as electronic monitoring. That's what it said in English, electronic monitoring. This last word "monitoring" was not translated into Croatian. It was only electronic that was translated into Croatian, and the other word was retained as monitoring is Croatian. So it sounds like science fiction, when you say it in Croatian "monitoring"; so perhaps he wasn't aware of what it was like. Perhaps if you show him this device he would know what it is all about. This sounds like from outer space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I really say that you know how to say things at the right time. All right. That's enough of that. I want to tell the witness that I'm paying particular attention to the way he answers, and I'm also speaking for my colleague. And if we were to count the number of times when the witness says he does not remember, he doesn't have a good memory, doesn't have the technical capabilities, he was not at the briefing, it is a bit worrisome. That is what I want to say. This is 12 days, now, we have been on this issue, and my responsibility is to move the trial forward.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 527, 527A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a retraction of a verbal protest dated the 22nd of April 1993 that was signed by Colonel Blaskic; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a copy of this went to the operations and training body of, over which you were the commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was translated to me saying that I was the commander of a unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. It may have been my improper, or inaccurate question. In the lower left-hand corner it says a copy of this goes to ONO; that's you, isn't it? I mean you told us during your direct examination when you wrote ONO on there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go through this. It says, "On April 22nd, 1993 at 2030 hours we protested verbally because you fired three shells in the town of Vitez. During the conversations we received a protest that we had fired six shells on the town of Zenica. Since we know for certain that our units did not shell the town, we requested that our military intelligence service provide the correct information regarding the place where the shells had been fired, based on electronic surveillance data." It just says, "On the basis of the data obtained, it was established that the Chetniks had fired three shells on the town of Vitez, and another three shells on the town of Travnik from their positions in Travica, they also shelled the town of Zenica from the positions in Kraljevo Guvno. In the view of the above-mentioned, we regret the confusion that ensued, and we would hereby like to retract our verbal protest and offer our apology." My question for you is: According to this letter, Colonel Blaskic has confirmed that he concluded where the shells were fired from, based on electronic surveillance data. Now, you were in the headquarters; what is this electronic surveillance data that Colonel Blaskic is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was in the staff. This equipment, this equipment, together with the intelligence department, was apart from the staff. This was a department led by Ivica Zeljko, and physically they were three or four kilometres away from us, and I really don't know what kind of equipment they had available. Perhaps it is a shame for me to say so as a trained officer, but I really didn't know what kind of devices we had available. You should bear in mind that I came on the 1st of November, so I had been there only four months in the command, and I'm going to admit what is true. After the war, I mean until the present day, I do not know where this equipment is and what its possibilities are. Perhaps this is due to my modest technical education, but that's the way things are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, turning to the shelling on the 19th, of Zenica, 1993, did any electronic surveillance data come to the headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, that indicated where those shells were fired from? And if so, what was that electronic surveillance data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The data that are mentioned in this letter by General Blaskic were received by him personally, not by myself. And he wrote what he had received. I would really be happy if I could speak about this equipment now and say what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you got a copy of this letter, and my last question on this vein is: Was the issue of the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April discussed by General Blaskic with you and the other officers in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, General Blaskic did talk to the commander of the division in order to check. And what information did I have? I had the information that we had not done this. And to tell you the truth, quite frankly, I wasn't interested in it any longer. And these data that are in this report, these possibilities did exist, and the shelling of Zenica and the shelling of Vitez, from the positions where the artillery of the army of Republika Srpska was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander that Blaskic talked to when he asked if these shells had been fired? What's that commander's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Bartinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, did Blaskic gather any electronic surveillance data from the shelling on the 19th and provide it to the 3rd Corps in order to prove that they had, HVO had not actually fired this weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this report, which is written to the Monitoring Mission, it is obvious that Mr. Blaskic did ask his assistant for intelligence affairs, and what he ascertained is written in this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With all due respect, Brigadier, this is a different shelling. I'm talking about the shelling on the 19th, not the shelling after that. I'm talking about the shelling of Zenica on the 19th. I'm asking you, did, to your knowledge, Blaskic gather electronic surveillance data to prove that the HVO did not shell Zenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was not aware of the General having collected this information. That is what it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this report that we are discussing now, where electronic surveillance is mentioned, and obviously we can't define what it is, we are talking about six shells on Zenica. Zenica was shelled on the 19th with six shells. So I believe that it is not two shellings of Zenica that we're talking about, but one single shelling of Zenica that is mentioned here, the shelling of Zenica with six shells on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have the documentation to clarify the point now, but I will provide the documentation. It's simply a different shelling, it's not the shelling that took place on the 19th, and it is an issue that we can discuss based on the documentation thereafter, but it's a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think it would be better to have the documents, in order to clarify the discussion. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you aware that the HVO and Colonel Blaskic blamed this shelling on the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I know that the shelling was not carried out by the HVO, and there were three armies in that area, there was no one else to do the shelling but the army of Republika Srpska. We didn't think that the army would shell itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, the Bosnian Serb army objected to that; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of what the army of the Bosnian Serbs did, as regards the shelling of Zenica on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a letter, sir, if I could move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 528, 528A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an order that came from the Commander Lieutenant Colonel Bozo Pulic (Phoen) of the 27th Motorised Brigade of the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska, and it's dated, I believe the original is the 27th; however, the translation has a question mark next to the 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 27 April, excuse me, 27 May, 1993. Let me just read a bit of this letter, Brigadier. It says, "Negotiations with the Ustashe. Order: We received the strictly confidential order number 0/2-448 from the GS main staff of the VRS Republic of Srpska army which regulates the following. It has been noticed that the Ustashe have been turning to units and commands of the VRS requesting support in the forms of weapons, ammunition, fire support, care for the wounded and use of our territory to evacuate forces and people in the regions where they are threatened by Muslims. "We have noted incidents of contacts being made with the Ustashe in the form of some kind of cooperation on lower levels which causes us more harm than good. And as a result, Ustashes are moving around our territory without the knowledge or approval of the Corps command. "On the other hand, Ustashe officials at the highest political, military and religious levels are blaming Serbs for the crimes of the HVO against the Muslims, and statements given to the mass media and approaches to international institutions. "They have announced that our forces targeted Zenica in order to blame the Serbs for the conflict with the Muslims. They have officially blamed the Serbs for the massacre of 500 Muslims in the Vitez area, even though UNPROFOR statements clearly confirm that the Croats are responsible." And you can gladly read the balance of this Brigadier. Were you made aware at any time directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President, I apologise. I would suggest that first and foremost we leave the witness enough time to read the entire document. And I think it would also be interesting for the Court to familiarise itself with the entire document, because that is where it exactly says where there was cooperation with the Serbs; and that was not Vitez, mind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can turn to where the cooperation was. I was trying to short circuit and talk about Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue reading, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next paragraph. "The Croatian Christian union organised a so-called scientific convention in Zagreb where the highest political, state and religious representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the so-called Bosnia-Herzegovina, Albania, Austria --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I'm sorry, once again. I'm sorry, I apologise for saying something all the time, but the translation said the Croatian Christian units. There is the Croatian Christian union, which is a political organisation, and the interpretation it sounded like a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I, myself, have seen the words union, yes, the Croatian Christian union. That's what it says in the transcript. All right. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Croatian Christian union organised a so-called scientific convention in Zagreb with the highest political, state and religious representatives of the Republic Croatia and so-called Bosnia-Herzegovina, Albania, Austria, prominent persons and leaders of extremist anti-Serbian parties of Kosovo, Visanjak (phoen), Macedonia, Bulgaria, Germany, et cetera, were present. "The purpose of the convention was to study and coordinate measures to join all these countries in a unified front in the battle against Serbs and Serbian. "The objective of Croatian politicians is to recreate the NDH, independent state of Croatia, within its historic borders, the Drina River, where Serbs would not have a place even as a minority. "To this end, and under the umbrella of the highest political bodies of the Republic of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, the so-called Muslim Democratic Party has been formed. Its head is Arman Pohar (phoen), who is committed to a common existence with Croats and a joint struggle against the Serbs. "We stress that Ustashes tend to ask for help and cooperation in areas where they are threatened by Muslims, Usora, Konjic, Vares, Kiseljak, Tuzla. At the same time they are forcibly trying to realise their aims, Orasje, eastern Herzegovina, et cetera, and other parts of the front. Simultaneously they are also negotiating with the Serbs in areas -- I'm sorry, negotiating with the Muslims, I'm sorry. "Simultaneously negotiating with the Muslims in areas in which they might be threatened. "This indicates that they are negotiating with us to save themselves if the relations with the Muslims take an inconvenient turn. Keeping in mind the above mentioned objectives and actions, I order the following: Should Ustashes contact you for help and cooperation, stress that the fundamental obstacle in cooperation is the behaviour of their officials at the highest level. The crimes they committed against the Serbian people and their attributing to the Serbs all the crimes that Croats committed in the conflict with the Muslims. "2. Bear in mind that a joint struggle against the Serbs is the basic platform of Croats and Muslims in their endeavours to overcome conflicts between them. "3. Instruct them to forward their requests for help and cooperation through their highest military and political representatives and inform them that agreements on any future cooperation must be made at the highest military and state level. "4. Report any announced contact with the Ustashes, requests submitted by them, et cetera, to the VRS general staff. "5. In your contacts you must strive to acquire exhaustive intelligence data on Croatian and Muslim forces; size, structure, condition, weaponry, intentions, bearing in mind the interests of the VRS and the Republic of Srpska. In your contacts with Ustashes, prevent any classified military information being leaked. The delegation for possible negotiations will be named by corps commanders. The delegation must include a member of the intelligence and security body. "7. Any contact with the enemy or attempts to make such contact must be reported in detail to the corps command, the organ for intelligence and security affairs, for their information, accompanied by your opinion and proposal for measures. "8. Individual and unplanned contacts with the Ustashes are forbidden, as are agreements at lower levels. Such occurrences must, therefore, be prevented vigorously by the command and appropriate measures must be taken against those responsible. "9. Battalion commanders and the commanding officers of independent companies are responsible to me for carrying out this order." Signed by Lieutenant Colonel Bozo Pulic. On this particular document, Brigadier, did it come to the attention of the headquarters that the Bosnian Serbs did object to being blamed for the shelling of Zenica, as well as being blamed for any of the crimes that took place in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that in a conversation with a British officer that Colonel Blaskic blamed what happened in Ahmici on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to Defence Exhibit 321, which is the map, and if we could put this on the easel? Brigadier, taking a look at Exhibit 321, and again, I realise we're that only talking about the major areas of conflict and the major areas of artillery fire, there would appear to be significant artillery fire in the Vitez municipality on the 19th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not artillery fire. The army shelled all these places that are marked on this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I'm talking -- we're not understanding each other. The arrows reflect artillery fire by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the circles represent major areas of conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are areas where, during the day, there was larger-scale shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, Brigadier, that in the Vitez area, according to your map, there appears to be artillery fire taking place in at least one, two, three, four, five, six different areas, and that includes downtown Vitez; would you agree with that? If you want to get up and count the arrows, I mean, you're welcome to go up and count the arrows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need for me to do that. Intensive shelling, intensive shelling, the strongest shelling that day in Vitez was in Kruscica, in the town of Vitez, and along the defence lines held by the HVO units. The arrows from this little circle that says Vitez, there are one, two, three of them, they show the shelling along the defence lines. Because the positions that are marked here, that is where the defence line of the HVO is vis-à-vis the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you also have the town of Vitez being shelled; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I can ask the question again. You also have the town of Vitez being shelled; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was shelled in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say now what particular facility was shelled that day, but shells were falling on the town of Vitez. During the war, that is to say, from the 16th until the 19th, the greatest effects of the shelling were seen on the hotel, the post office, the municipality building and -- I can't remember the name of the building where the health centre was. Those were the effects of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the shelling on Vitez continue on the 20th and the 21st and the 22nd and the 23rd, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to data or, rather, according to the things I remember, because I did not prepare myself in terms of Vitez Brigade, the 20th and the 21st and the 22nd, those were the days when the cease-fire was to start, and on those days, the shelling had practically, I think, subsided, or if there was shelling, then it was only on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let's talk about the area on the 19th, the area that is being shelled on the 19th. This is quite a significant amount of shelling taking place in Vitez on the 19th, and again, I want to turn your attention to Defence Exhibit 345. Again, as we did yesterday, Brigadier, I would ask you to take a look at chart for the 19th and I would ask you to tell this Court how many people were killed on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence proposes, whichever number the Prosecution puts forward, we accept. Whatever number the Prosecution states, the witness can say "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you counted the number of victims. How many did you count?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, or do you want to count them again? In principle, the Defence agrees with you, but you are not the one who is accused, but do you agree with the figure one? Do you have faith in the Prosecutor's number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is data which is on the list, and I'm not in a position to give any other number because this would just -- a lot of time would go by. It would be guesswork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It has been noted that you can count up to one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will take as the figure one since -- it is a very low number of casualties, which is a very good thing. It is now twenty after five. What is the question that you want to ask in respect of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just about through that particular area. I will just put on the record, so that my counting is not inaccurate, the only individual on this record that I find killed on the 19th of April is number 196 in Exhibit 345, Pero Miskovic. That's the only one that I find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Pero Miskovic. I see the place indicated is Santici?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, are there not others who are indicated on this document as having died on that date but in other places?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think so, Judge. On the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, I see, 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, you may be right. I have some other months. Nineteenth, but some other months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You were very successful in your evaluations, Mr. Kehoe. You can continue now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Brigadier, back to Exhibit 456/50. I'm sorry we didn't keep this out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 19th April, 1993, order of Colonel Blaskic at 2140 hours. Judge Shahabuddeen, I stand to be corrected if my counting is wrong on that but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't worry. He will correct you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: ... that your counting is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Let's go on for another six minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, before we talk about this, where were you and where was Colonel Blaskic during this entire time? And I'm talking about the 16th, the 17th, the 18th, the 19th, the 20th. Where were you? Were you in the Hotel Vitez the entire time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire time I was in the operative centre in the Hotel Vitez, and I worked there as far as time allowed, I slept there and had my meals there, because I said that on the 16th of April, there were only seven of us in the command headquarters, so that I had none of my associates there and I had to do everything myself, within the region of the things I was in charge with, and General Blaskic was in the hotel at the same time. He sat -- that is to say, he had his table at the operative headquarters in the same -- and he had an office in the same building. And it was his personal assessment when he would come to the headquarters. When he did not consider that this was necessary, he would go to his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Blaskic went to Zenica for the meeting on the 21st of -- or, actually, he went to BRITBAT and also Zenica on the 21st to cease-fire meetings, didn't he? The 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we wish to be precise, as far as I recall, the meeting in Zenica was on the 20th, and in Nova Bila, it was on the 21st, as a continuation of the previous meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can agree that the document that we talked about previously was on the 21st of April, based on the Defence document. Up until going to that meeting in Bila and Zenica, were Blaskic and you both in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us turn back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me be more precise. Until he left for the meeting, General Blaskic was constantly in the hotel, and after the meeting, I, myself, as I began in the morning on the 16th until the cease-fire had actually taken into effect, I was and remained in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the evening of the 19th, and let me direct your attention back to Exhibit 456/50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. If we wish to ascertain when the meeting was, I think the meeting was on the 20th, and if we're going to speak of the night when General Blaskic was at the meeting in Zenica, then we should have in mind the time term 20th and not the 19th. If there is document that states that it was the 19th, there is no problem. I remember the events, what happened at the time when he went to Zenica; that is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we will get to that in a little bit when I think we will agree, after we show and refresh your recollection with some documentation, that the meeting in Zenica was the 21st. But nevertheless, let's turn our attention back to Exhibit 456/50 before we conclude for today, and I would ask you to take a look at paragraph one. We're not going to focus on Gomionica here but on the second part of the sentence. It says: "You must take Gomionica tonight or in the early morning because the main forces of the Muslim armed forces are at Busovaca which is being attacked today by the main forces of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although certainly unsuccessfully." So Blaskic is telling the 3rd Corps that the main force of 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is attacking on the evening of the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not so. Let us read the whole text once again. "You must take Gomionica tonight or in the early morning because the main forces of the MOS are at Busovaca." That means on the day, the 19th, the General is writing on 21. He is saying what went before in the course of the day. So if you write a report at 2100 hours, then you say what happened until that time, 9.00 p.m. You cannot write something that you suppose happened. If you write something that you suppose happened, then you say so. But it is obvious from the map and the data that I have at what places the BH army attacked on that particular day in Busovaca, and they are the following places: Doboj, Putis, Gradina, Solokovici, Milavice, Kapak, Polonj, Ocehnic, Prosija. Those are the places where there was fighting in the course of the 19th of April. And in Vitez there was fighting, infantry fighting, in Sivrino Selo. That is a village. It is some 200 metres away from the Busovaca-Vitez main road, and that is where the lines remained as they were established on the 17th. But there was fighting over those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I apologise if my question was inaccurate. All I'm asking you is, by 2140 hours, the main force of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 3rd Corps, is attacking the Busovaca forces; isn't that what Colonel Blaskic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says, what is written, and that is our assessment because the forces of those attacks were such that we assessed that they were the main force. If we knew exactly who was attacking us and where they would attack us, we would be more successful in defending ourselves, so that is an observation on the basis of what was happening on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I think the prior confusion was as a result of my question more than anything else. I'm just about to go into another subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the interpreters have been working for a long time. I would like you to recall that tomorrow is our last day. How do you see the continuation of what we're doing? About an equivalent amount of time has been divided between the direct and the cross-examination, or the Prosecutor has taken a little bit more time. All right. You are now going beyond the time that was spent in direct examination, and you are to continue with your cross-examination. Can you give us an assessment of how much time you are going to need to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to try to do my best to finish this tomorrow, Mr. President, but I must say candidly, it's difficult to know. And I think that, without rehashing what's happened previously, I think, Mr. President, you've noted some of the difficulties that have taken place during cross. But I will endeavour to try to finish. I certainly would like to do so, as do my colleagues, and that is what we're hoping to do, but if we get to that point or not, I just don't know at this juncture, but that certainly is the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I spoke with my colleague. At least what I can say, and we all agree, that the 26th of October, Monday, the General will have to come back. I think things have to be clear. Unless the Defence does not want to conduct a rebuttal, but I don't think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I know that the scheduling of the Court is very difficult. Our request would be to try and finish the witness this week, even if we have to extend hours, because to send him back to the federal army to serve in the middle of his testimony we think is, as we said at beginning of the testimony, is a very difficult situation to put the witness in. I understand we all have obligations, there is limitations on staff, spacing, and so forth, but that's our position, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like you to answer my question, also, Mr. Hayman. I wanted to know whether you're going to conduct a rebuttal. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but very directly and very efficiently, so we're not going to take up a lot of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sure that you will get very specific and direct answers from your witness. I have no doubt about that. Nonetheless, it is true - now I turn to my colleague - that one simply cannot think about finishing tomorrow. The Judges have many questions that they want to ask; and therefore, I think that hypothetically we can say that the General must make arrangements to be here on Monday, the 26th. The 26th, Monday. Or else the witness will remain in The Hague for the week. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President, there would be certain difficulties for the witness to remain in The Hague, perhaps, but we suggest that this Trial Chamber, and you as its President, give an express order to the witness to appear on a given date in the Court, and so, if he has this order, then he will be able to take it to his superiors and be allowed to come here and remain here. I think that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there would be no objection to that. All right. The order will be issued based on Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I think we're now going to suspend the hearing. Those things are clear. Tomorrow you will continue the cross-examination, Mr. Kehoe, and try to finish it, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. And I wish everybody a good evening. Tomorrow we will resume at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
